q: Does this situation justify a MAYDAY?
a: Yes — grave and imminent danger to boat and crew
o: No — not until the crew has to abandon ship
No — first ask the coastguard if it qualifies
Only if another vessel is in sight to help
why: MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger needing immediate help — an uncontrolled fire is exactly that.

q: Your yacht Blue Dolphin is sinking and you pick up the microphone on channel 16. How does your distress call begin?
a: MAYDAY ×3, THIS IS, Blue Dolphin ×3
o: THIS IS, Blue Dolphin ×3, then MAYDAY ×3
MAYDAY once, THIS IS, Blue Dolphin once
ALL STATIONS ×3, THIS IS, Blue Dolphin ×3
why: Distress call: MAYDAY three times, THIS IS, the boat's name three times (with call sign or MMSI).

q: You have said MAYDAY three times and THIS IS Blue Dolphin three times, with your call sign. What do you say next?
a: MAYDAY, Blue Dolphin, then your position
o: Your problem first, then your position
Number of people aboard, then position
OVER, and wait for a reply first
why: The message opens with MAYDAY and the name once more; position comes first — rescuers need it most.

q: In which order do you give these four items in your message?
a: Position, distress, help, persons
o: Persons, position, distress, help
Distress, help, position, persons
Position, persons, help, distress
why: Order: position, nature of distress, assistance required, persons on board, then other useful information.

fig.title: Your MAYDAY message
lines: Help: need pumps and a tow

q: Your plotter has died and you will give your position relative to something on the chart. Which reference do you choose?
a: A charted lighthouse or headland nearby
o: The nearest anchored yacht you can see
The name of the beach taverna ashore
The marina you left this morning
why: Bearing and distance must be from a charted point that rescuers can find on their own chart.

q: You read this off the plotter for your MAYDAY. How do you say the position on air?
a: Latitude first, then longitude, N and E
o: Longitude first, then latitude, E and N
Latitude only — that is enough at sea
Rounded to whole degrees: 38 N 24 E
why: Position by coordinates: latitude first, then longitude, each with N/S or E/W.

q: Is a MAYDAY the right call?
a: No — there is no grave and imminent danger
o: Yes — any engine failure at sea is distress
Yes — but sent on low power only
Yes — if you cannot reach port by dark
why: No grave and imminent danger, no MAYDAY: sail on, or ask for help with a lower-priority call.

q: You have sent your MAYDAY on 16 and, after listening for a while, nobody answers. What do you do?
a: Repeat it, and use other means: flares, EPIRB
o: Wait a full hour before calling again
Move to channel 6 and call only there
Stop transmitting to save the battery
why: An unanswered MAYDAY is repeated; meanwhile raise the alarm by every other means you have.

q: After your MAYDAY you hear: "MAYDAY Blue Dolphin, this is Olympia Radio, RECEIVED MAYDAY". What does it tell you?
a: Your distress call has been received
o: Your call was unclear — send it again
You must now downgrade to PAN-PAN
Olympia Radio is calling another vessel
why: RECEIVED MAYDAY is the acknowledgement: your distress has been heard and help is being organised.

q: Nobody else seems to be responding to this call. What do you do on the radio now?
a: Send a MAYDAY RELAY on 16 for Selene
o: Acknowledge Selene and keep to your course
Keep silent — it is not your distress
Call Selene on channel 6 to check first
why: A MAYDAY that nobody acknowledges, when you cannot help yourself: relay it with MAYDAY RELAY.

fig.title: Heard on 16
lines: Selene is 18 miles off — too far for you

q: You are relaying another yacht's distress from your own yacht, Aura. How does your call begin?
a: MAYDAY RELAY ×3, ALL STATIONS ×3, THIS IS, Aura ×3
o: MAYDAY ×3, THIS IS, the other yacht ×3
MAYDAY RELAY ×3, ALL STATIONS ×3, THIS IS, the other yacht ×3
PAN-PAN ×3, THIS IS, Aura ×3
why: A relay opens MAYDAY RELAY three times, then the station addressed (a coast station or ALL STATIONS), THIS IS and your own name — never pose as the casualty.

q: You are sure this was a distress signal. Which radio call do you send?
a: MAYDAY RELAY, with what you saw and where
o: MAYDAY in your own boat's name
PAN-PAN, as you do not know her name
Nothing until you know who fired it
why: A vessel in distress that cannot call for herself: you send a MAYDAY RELAY on her behalf.

q: Before you step into the raft, what do you do about the VHF radios?
a: Take the handheld into the raft with you
o: Stay below on the fixed set to the end
Leave the handheld — it won't work in a raft
Leave the handheld aboard, still calling
why: A handheld in the raft lets you talk to rescuers as they close in.

q: The anchor will not hold again in time. Which call do you make, and when?
a: MAYDAY now — the danger is grave and imminent
o: PAN-PAN now, MAYDAY once she hits the rocks
A routine call to the marina for a tow
Wait — try to re-anchor first, then call
why: Do not wait for the impact: grave and imminent danger means MAYDAY now.

fig.title: Lee shore
lines: Six aboard, no room to sail off

q: Which call do you make?
a: MAYDAY — a person in the water is in grave danger
o: PAN-PAN — the yacht itself is not in danger
No call until you have searched for an hour
SÉCURITÉ asking boats to keep a lookout
why: A person overboard and lost from sight is in grave and imminent danger: MAYDAY.

fig.title: Crew overboard
lines: Lost sight of her in the waves

q: The skipper is unconscious, the boat is on fire, and you have no radio certificate. May you send the MAYDAY?
a: Yes — anyone aboard may send a distress call
o: No — only a certificate holder may transmit
Only with the owner's consent by phone
Only from the handheld, not the fixed set
why: In distress anyone may use the radio; the certificate rule never stops a MAYDAY.

q: The coast station is handling your MAYDAY for a fire, but you have now put the fire out and need no help. What do you do?
a: Tell the coast station at once that you need no help
o: Say nothing — the coastguard will work it out
Switch the radio off to keep 16 clear
Send a SÉCURITÉ saying that you are safe
why: Rescuers keep coming until told: tell the station controlling the distress that you are safe.

q: Which important items are missing from this message?
a: Help needed and number of persons aboard
o: The skipper's name and home port
The time and the weather at the scene
Destination and last port of call
why: A distress message gives position, nature of distress, assistance required and persons on board.

fig.title: Overheard MAYDAY
lines: MAYDAY Aura, 2 miles south of Poros

q: With no GPS fix, you use the lighthouse to find your place. How do you report your position in the MAYDAY?
a: 150° from the lighthouse, 4 miles
o: 330° from the lighthouse, 4 miles
4 miles from the lighthouse, no bearing
Your last GPS fix, an hour old
why: Bearing is given FROM the landmark: the reciprocal of your bearing to it (330° − 180° = 150°).

fig.note: Bearing from your boat to the light

q: You have just finished giving your MAYDAY message. How do you end it, and then what?
a: Say OVER, then listen on 16 for an answer
o: Say OUT, then switch off to save power
Say OVER, then change to a working channel
Repeat it at once, without listening
why: End with OVER and listen: the coast station or a nearby vessel will acknowledge on 16.
